correctness.rationale: The explicit witness is an actual positive CRT residue in a full interval of length \(aP_a(K)\). Reducing any representation modulo \(a\) gives \(y\equiv-1\) with \(2\le y\le K\); a prime factor \(p\mid y\) is disjoint from \(a\) and divides \(P_a(K)\mid N\), so \(p\mid x\). This exhausts all representations, not merely enumerated ones. At fixed \(a\), the prime number theorem implies \(\log P_a(K)=K+o(K)\); taking \(K=\lfloor(1-\varepsilon)\log b\rfloor\) gives \(P_a(K)=o(b)\) and the liminf at least one. The 408 exact finite enumeration checks support but do not prove the limit.

originality.rationale: Ding–Wang–Zhang (2025) study precisely the same primitive-representation Frobenius number and prove upper and lower estimates of orders ab(log ab)^2 and ab; neither bound entails an asymptotic lower bound of order b log b at fixed a. Jaffe (2026) studies the same definition and its special cases. Shimizu (2026) proves a fixed factor-four lower bound using a related finite CRT prime-cover argument, which does not imply divergence relative to the ordinary Frobenius number. No checked source states the fixed-a logarithmic liminf, but the proof-method proximity and incomplete primary full-text access leave historical priority provisional.
residual_risks: Full PDFs of Ding–Wang–Zhang and Shimizu were not obtained for line-by-line inspection; an implicit stronger lower bound in an appendix cannot be absolutely excluded.
A small-prime Chinese remainder method already appears in Shimizu; an unindexed generalization with growing prime cutoff may exist.
No literature search proves global novelty or independent verification.

value.rationale: The result establishes an explicit, motivated growth dichotomy for the newly studied primitive Frobenius invariant: the fixed a=1,2 cases are linear, whereas all fixed a>=3 have g/b→infinity, quantitatively at least logarithmically. It strengthens the only retrieved general lower estimates from constant-factor to a growing factor, complementing an existing O_a(b log^2 b) upper bound and narrowing the genuine logarithmic exponent uncertainty. It is a theorem about all coprime b, not an arbitrarily selected numerical slice.
